coherence.reasons: Both follow a clean diagnosis-to-plan-to-first-moves pyramid, with titles that state conclusions and evidence that supports them. X has two internal tensions. Its governing thought says "not wages", yet its largest single lever is a $7.3M labor cut, more than twice the delivery fix it headlines. Its headline of 3.2% "clears the target" excludes the known 2027 wage rise, which its own backup shows drops the plan to 2.7%. Y's governing thought (2.9–3.1%, withdraw the 8% cut) matches what its bridge, options table, scenarios and board asks deliver, and its slide 3 hypothesis tree links the diagnosis to the plan. Y's framing of its own working hypothesis on that slide is slightly confusing but does not break the logic.

judgment.reasons: Both land on the answer key's preferred plan: a sized multi-lever plan with delivery repricing, pruning of losing promotions, shrink, private label, store exits and only targeted labor moves. Y weighs alternatives more fully. It sizes five options, including the management draft (0.9–1.7%), the plan without the three board-vote stores, and exiting home delivery (about +$6.4M, kept as a fallback for the owners). X dismisses most alternatives in a single line each. Y builds the 2027 wage step into the base case and admits the base lands at 2.9%, with a named stretch to 3.1%. X's base case leaves the wage rise out and relies on aggressive stretch levers (promotions back to 24%, shrink to 2.1%) that sit awkwardly with its own ValuMart defence. Y's labor move is smaller and safer: a net 2% cut with reinvestment and a reversal trigger. X's net 4% taken only in Q3–Q4 stores implies cuts of 8% or more in those stores while assuming shrink stays flat. Y also deducts volume loss from the promotion cut, budgets $20.1M of one-time cost against the $25M cap, sets stage gates and contingencies, and gives a low/base/high range. X counts only the $7.5M lease exit as one-time cost.

evidence.reasons: Both get the critical numbers right: labor at about 13% of the decline, the wage/hours decomposition, the −$10.4M e-commerce drag, −$12.34 per delivered order, the fee-test value of $2.5–2.8M and the $6.6M store-exit gain. Both reject the 6.1% e-commerce claim and the category team's correlation. X has some strengths: it rebuilds the fulfillment line for all three years, and its sums are accurate. It also makes weaker inferences. It reads −4.2% comps near ValuMart as showing promotions "have not held off ValuMart" with no counterfactual. It sizes the promotion reset with no volume loss. It assumes zero shrink effect from a concentrated cut in Q3–Q4 stores. It implies no one-time costs beyond the lease exits. Y gives the bridge in dollars and explains why it sums to $35.4M rather than $32.6M (sales growth). It tests the category team's claim quantitatively (break-even at 2.3 pt of extra promotional share) and nets out double counting by using a reduced sales base. Y's weak spots are the vendor-funding sizing, the one-time cost allowances and the assumption that half the wage step is recovered in prices. All are assumptions, but each is flagged, and vendor funding is set to zero in the low case.

revision.reasons: Both correctly revise management's view. They show wages rose 9.4% but hours per sale fell, so labor explains only about an eighth of the decline, and they replace the 8% blanket cut because of the shrink link. Y goes further on both halves of the management plan. It carries the draft through to an FY2028 outcome ($13–26M, 0.9–1.7%) to show it cannot reach the target. It also addresses the e-commerce freeze directly: keep growth frozen but reprice, because a freeze alone leaves the loss in place. Y keeps what the evidence supports, a small targeted trim where Q3 and Q4 shrink are nearly equal, and includes the upcoming wage step in the plan. X does not address the freeze. It also retains a labor cut that is half the size of management's and is its single largest lever, which keeps more of the original hypothesis than the shrink evidence comfortably supports. Y's slide 3 tests its own working hypothesis rather than management's, a minor framing flaw, but it shows real updating.

overall.reasons: Both are strong documents that reach a defensible conclusion with a quantified bridge and levers that add up. Y would serve the CEO better before the board. It is honest that the base case lands at 2.9% after the wage step and names the stretch that closes the gap. It budgets one-time costs against the $25M cap, compares sized options including the management draft and a delivery exit, and builds in traffic loss from promotion cuts. It also gives gates, contingencies, a downside range and six explicit board decisions. X is rigorous and its arithmetic is sound, but its headline of 3.2% depends on excluding a known wage rise, on a larger labor cut assumed to carry no shrink risk, and on a promotion reset with no volume loss. That makes its plan look safer than it is.
